text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD

- Former Women's Affairs Minister Johanna Dohnal has founded a committee to push for the introduction of the demands in a recent petition for more women's rights. The government plans to start talks with the initiators of the petitions.
- Social Democrats have sold their stake in the Austrian National Bank to Bank Austria's Industrieholding.
- Austria wants to introduce new strategies for European structural politics. The main focus is to centre on eastern expansion and transit problems.

- Gustav Raab, the finance ministry's representative for information on the introduction of the European Union's single currency euro, has cancelled an agreement with the European Commission not to hold different views on the euro.

- Hannes Androsch, new owner of Austria's salt producer Salinen AG, has offered the second bidder, agricultural group Agrana, a cooperation deal. Employees and the management of Salinen AG are to hold a 30-percent share of their company.

- Herbert Hax, chief of Germany's expert committee on the euro, said the "restriction to a fixed date for the start of European Economic and Monetary Union was a mistake". He does not expect Germany to meet the Maastricht criteria in time.
- Regional energy povider EVN's first half results fell 14 percent, compared to the same period last year.
DIE PRESSE
- The City of Vienna's liability for Bank Austria saves the bank more than 100 million schillings, says investment bank Goldman Sachs.
- Chancellor Viktor Klima is pleased by the result of the two petitions against gene-manipulation and for women's rights.
- Banks have offered sports goods maker HTM to reduce interest by 300 million schillings if the company hands over shares as a security.
- Hannes Androsch and Raiffeisen Landesbank Oberoesterreich plan to make the Salinen AG the new market leader in central Europe.
- Trade with Italy reached a new record level of 113 billion schillings. Austria mainly exported high-quality goods.
KURIER
- Municipalities plan to raise property taxes in order to reduce labour costs.
- The Finance Ministry annually earns around seven billion schillings in taxes from the national lottery.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- Conservative state leaders demand the authority to issue directives to the members of their parliamentary state chamber.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Conservatives criticise the new minimum corporate tax of five percent on capital. The People's Party demands minimum corporate taxes from 15,000 schillings to 100,000 schillings.
- Austria Tabak, which is due to be privatised this year, has become Europe's largest cigratte selling company by completely taking over Germany's tobaccoland for five billion schillings.
